1051.title: Christmas night
1051.hook: shepherds in the fields see the sky fill with angels (Luke 2:8–14)
1051.howItsDone: Luke's story of the shepherds is read in churches at Christmas, and some churches hold services late on Christmas Eve, where the angels' words are read and sung.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was al-Qadr, and your line was better than a thousand months. Today, a second night of wonder, from a different book, set in a field.

Night shift. Not in a hospital or a warehouse, but out in a field, with a flock of sheep that can't be left alone. Somebody has to stay awake in case of wolves or thieves or a lamb that wanders. So a few men sit by the animals in the dark, talking low or not at all. Nobody important. Nobody expecting anything. That's where Luke's Gospel sets the night Jesus is born: not in a palace or a temple, but out with the night shift.
screen: `NIGHT SHIFT, IN A FIELD.` → `NOBODY EXPECTING ANYTHING.` → `LUKE SETS THE SCENE HERE.`

segments.voice: First, who gets the news. The King James Version puts it simply: "And there were in the same country shepherds abiding in the field, keeping watch over their flock by night." Jesus has just been born in Bethlehem, and Luke's first announcement of that birth doesn't go to rulers or priests. It goes to men keeping watch over sheep. Second, the light. "And, lo, the angel of the Lord came upon them, and the glory of the Lord shone round about them: and they were sore afraid." Sore afraid means terrified. In this story, that's the first reaction to awe, and Luke doesn't hide it. Third, the message. The angel's first words are "Fear not," and then: "for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people." Christian tradition hears in it the heart of Christmas: the child born that night is the Savior, and the news is for everyone, starting with the people in the field. Then a crowd of angels fills the sky, praising God: "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men." Fourth, what happens next. When the angels go, the shepherds don't stay put and argue. They say to each other, let's go to Bethlehem and see. And they go. One more thing: Luke never says what season it was. The winter fields of carols and cards come from the time of year the feast is kept, not from the text. What Luke gives is a dark field, ordinary men at work, and a sky that suddenly won't stay quiet.
screen: `THE NEWS GOES TO THE NIGHT SHIFT.` · `SORE AFRAID: TERRIFIED.` · `FEAR NOT. GOOD TIDINGS FOR ALL PEOPLE.` · `LET'S GO AND SEE.` · then, large: `GLORY TO GOD IN THE HIGHEST.`

segments.voice: Imagine the cold on your face, the dark around you, the sky wide overhead, and picture yourself as one of those people on the night shift, not waiting for anything, just keeping watch. If you pray, you can say the angels' line, glory to God in the highest; if you don't, just keep watch and see what the night offers.
Christmas night. Luke's dark field, where the first news of Jesus's birth comes to shepherds keeping watch by night. Today's word.
Your line: shepherds in the fields. The news went first to the people nobody was watching. See you in the morning.

1052.title: The mid-autumn moon
1052.hook: Chinese families gather to admire the full moon with mooncakes
1052.howItsDone: Families keep the Mid-Autumn Festival by gathering for a meal, sharing mooncakes, lighting lanterns and admiring the full moon; family members who are far apart sometimes call one another or send pictures of the moon.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Christmas night, and your line was shepherds in the fields. Tonight's wonder has no angels in it: just a moon, a table, and the people around it.

Someone is cutting the mooncakes into wedges so there's enough for everyone, each one round, heavy, stamped on top with a pattern. Paper lanterns hang in the yard or on the balcony. Grandparents, cousins, the uncle who always arrives late. And at some point in the evening, everybody goes quiet and looks up, because that's what the night is for. Families across China, and Chinese families far from China, keep a festival in the middle of autumn built around one thing: the full moon, admired together.
screen: `MOONCAKES CUT INTO WEDGES.` → `EVERYONE LOOKS UP.` → `A FESTIVAL BUILT AROUND THE MOON.`

segments.voice: First, the shape of things. The Mid-Autumn Festival falls on a full-moon night in the middle of autumn, counted by the old lunar calendar. The moon is round, the cakes are round, and the family sits around the table. Roundness, tradition says, means being whole, being together, nobody missing. Second, the story people tell. There's a legend, told in many versions, of Chang'e, a woman who drank an elixir of immortality and floated up to live on the moon, leaving her husband on the earth below. So on this night, some say, she looks down, and people look up toward her: a story about separation, kept at a festival about being together. Third, the poets. One short poem by Li Bai goes something like this: moonlight falls by my bed, so pale I take it for frost on the ground; I lift my head and look at the bright moon; I lower my head and think of home. Another poet, Su Shi, wrote on a mid-autumn night while missing his brother. He ends with a wish that, though far apart, they might live long and share the moon's beauty together. Fourth, why it moves people. The moon gives the same light to everyone who can see it. Family at the table, and family who couldn't make it home, look at the same moon at roughly the same time. The festival turns the sky into a meeting place. Awe, here, isn't a lonely feeling on a mountaintop. It's shared, passed around like cake.

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you'd want at the table, near or far, and picture the moon, wherever it is right now, above the place they are: the same light on their roof as on yours. If you pray, you can hold them in prayer; if you don't, just let the moon connect you.

Your line: the full moon together. Far apart, two people can still share one moon. Day one thousand fifty-two, complete.

1053.title: The Perseid meteors
1053.hook: in August the Perseids streak across the northern sky
1053.howItsDone: People who watch the Perseids go somewhere dark on clear nights during the shower, lie back and let their eyes adjust; some Catholics in Europe connect the meteors with the feast of Saint Lawrence.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Zhongqiu, the mid-autumn moon, and your line was the full moon together. Tonight the sky moves faster than the moon ever does.

Lying on your back in the grass at midnight is a strange thing for a grown person to do. The ground is cold. Sitting up, your neck ached from craning; flat on the grass, it finally doesn't. For a long while, nothing. Then, out of the corner of your eye, a thin bright scratch across the dark, there and gone before you can point. Somebody next to you says, did you see that? In late summer, in the northern half of the world, the Perseids are the reason people lie down in fields.
screen: `FLAT ON YOUR BACK AT MIDNIGHT.` → `A BRIGHT SCRATCH ACROSS THE DARK.` → `DID YOU SEE THAT?`

segments.voice: First, what you're seeing. A shooting star isn't a star at all. Astronomers explain it as a tiny piece of dust, left behind by a comet, hitting the air so fast that it burns up in a streak of light. The earth passes through that comet's trail around the same season each year, they say, and for a stretch the sky is busy. The meteors seem to come from where the constellation Perseus stands, which is how they got their name. Second, another name. In parts of Europe the Perseids have been called the tears of Saint Lawrence, because they fall near the feast day of Lawrence, a deacon of the early church whom tradition remembers as a martyr. So the same streaks carry a Greek hero's name and a saint's tears, depending on who was looking up. Third, a psalm about names. A psalm in the Hebrew Bible goes further. In the King James words: "He telleth the number of the stars; he calleth them all by their names." In the psalm, naming the lights isn't only a human habit; every one is already known by name. For people who pray the psalm, that's part of the wonder: so much light, and none of it anonymous. Fourth, the wish. Some people make a wish on a shooting star. Where that custom began isn't in today's texts. It shows a simple instinct: when something bright and brief crosses the sky, people want to answer it. A wish, a prayer, a gasp, or just a hand on the arm of the person next to you.
screen: `NOT A STAR: A SPECK OF DUST.` · `THE TEARS OF SAINT LAWRENCE.` · `HE CALLETH THEM ALL BY THEIR NAMES.` · `SOMETHING BRIGHT AND BRIEF, ANSWERED.` · then, large: `A SHOOTING STAR.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and let your shoulders sink as if you were already lying in the grass. Hold the psalm's line lightly, he calleth them all by their names; shooting stars reward patience. If you pray, let the psalm be your prayer; if you don't, just wait, and watch.

1054.title: Awe close
1054.hook: fifty-six days of looking up; awe, the traditions agree, makes us humble, though they name its source differently
1054.howItsDone: Some Jews and Christians read the book of Job, including God's speech from the whirlwind, as a picture of awe before the Creator; some readers of Emerson and some people with no religious tradition also seek the same humbling in nature.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Perseid meteors, and your line was a shooting star. Today, the last day of the block on awe.

Fifty-six days. This block opened with a plain question: what is awe? Since then: Moses with his shoes off, a still small voice, the heavens declaring, Arjuna before the universal form, Pascal in infinite spaces, Emerson as a transparent eyeball. Then outside: sunrises, clouds, one tree, water, storms, a newborn, a sacred building visited as a guest. And these last days, a heartbeat, a sink full of dishes, an eclipse, and four nights of wonder. So what did it add up to?
screen: `WHAT IS AWE?` → `SCRIPTURES, POETS, SCIENTISTS.` → `FOUR NIGHTS OF WONDER.`

segments.voice: First, what kept happening. In story after story, awe made people smaller. Not crushed. Smaller, the way a person can feel at the edge of the ocean. Second, the voice from the whirlwind, which asked Job about the stars on the night-sky day. After Job has demanded answers for chapter after chapter, God finally speaks, and the first thing God does is ask a question. In the King James words: "Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? declare, if thou hast understanding." Job wanted an explanation. He's handed a question instead, and he comes out of it quiet. In Job's story, and in the Jewish and Christian reading of it, the source of awe is God. Third, the poet in the field. Emerson, standing on bare ground under an open sky, wrote: "I become a transparent eye-ball; I am nothing; I see all". In the same sentence he says the currents of the Universal Being circulate through him, and that he is part or particle of God: a God met in the woods and the open field, not a voice from a whirlwind. Some of this block's scientists found the same smallness with no God named: in the age of the stars, the length of time, the size of what's out there. Fourth, what's easy to miss. In these two, the smallness isn't the end. Job is humbled, and then his story goes on. Emerson says he's nothing and, in the same breath, that he sees all. The traditions name the source differently, and they don't have to agree. But in these stories, the people who felt awe came back lighter. Smaller, and somehow glad to be.
screen: `AWE MAKES PEOPLE SMALLER.` · `WHERE WAST THOU?` · `I AM NOTHING; I SEE ALL.` · `HUMBLED, AND LIGHTER.` · then, large: `SMALLER, AND GLAD.`

segments.voice: Lift your eyes to the sky through a window, or to the highest point in the room, and let one moment from this block come back on its own: a line, a night, a sunrise, a heartbeat. If you pray, give thanks to the source you believe in; if you don't, stay with the size of things, the smaller thing in the picture.
Universal form. Arjuna's vision, one of many names this block gave awe's source, each ending in the same humbling, lightening feeling. Today's word.

1055.title: Six questions, looked back
1055.hook: suffering, death, love, work, forgiveness, awe
1055.carry: which one is quietly carrying you
1055.howItsDone: People on a spiritual path of their own sometimes keep a journal and reread it at the end of a year; some synagogues read Ecclesiastes during the festival of Sukkot.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was universal form, and your line was smaller, and glad. That closed the last of this year's six blocks; now the year itself starts to close, with a look back.

Six words could sum up this whole year: suffering, death, love, work, forgiveness, awe. Say them slowly and they sound like the chapter titles of a life. A person hurts. Someone they love dies. They love, and get loved, imperfectly. They spend their days working at something. They get wronged, and they wrong people. And now and then, the sky opens. This year asked each of those as a question, and handed it to the traditions willing to answer. Today, the six side by side.
screen: `SIX WORDS FOR A YEAR.` → `CHAPTER TITLES OF A LIFE.` → `SIX QUESTIONS, SIDE BY SIDE.`

segments.voice: First, the questions themselves. Why do people suffer? What happens when someone dies? What is love? Why work? How do you forgive? And what do you do with wonder? None of these were asked to be solved. Each block brought voices from many traditions, scripture, philosophers, poets, scientists, and let them speak in their own words, each with its own name on it. Second, an old book that holds several at once. Ecclesiastes, in the Hebrew Bible, says in the King James words: "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven". And a few lines later: "A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance". The writer doesn't rank the seasons. Weeping and dancing both get their time, and this year gave suffering and awe, death and love, each a season of its own. Third, a poet's advice about questions. Rainer Maria Rilke, writing letters to a young poet who wanted answers, told him to be patient with everything unsolved in his heart, and to try to love the questions themselves. Don't hunt for answers that can't be given yet, he said. Live the questions, and maybe, gradually, you'll live your way into an answer. Fourth, why look back now. A year of big questions can blur. Looking back doesn't mean deciding who was right. It means noticing which question you're still carrying, which one you put down, and which one is quietly carrying you.

segments.voice: Settle, and say the first word inside: suffering. Wait for whatever comes, a note you kept or a moment from that block, then go on, death, love, work, forgiveness, awe, without judging what shows up or what doesn't. If you pray, offer each one up as it comes; if you don't, let each have its season.
Six questions. Suffering, death, love, work, forgiveness, awe: the year's questions, each given its own season, none of them solved. Today's word.

1056.title: Which voice surprised you
1056.hook: a tradition you didn't expect to learn from
1056.howItsDone: People on a spiritual path of their own sometimes read across traditions and keep each teaching's source attached; some keep a list of teachers and lines they're grateful for, as Marcus Aurelius did in the first book of the Meditations.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was six questions, and your line was which one is quietly carrying you. Today, from the questions to the voices that answered them.

A Stoic emperor on grief. A Sufi poet on love. A Zen saying about chopping wood. A psalm about still waters. A Sikh hymn, a Jewish blessing, a Hindu warrior on a battlefield, a Christian cook at a kitchen stove. This year put a lot of voices in one room, not all of them ones you expected. Maybe one of them stopped you: a line you didn't see coming, from a place you didn't expect to learn anything from.
screen: `A LOT OF VOICES IN ONE ROOM.` → `ONE OF THEM STOPPED YOU.` → `THE ONE YOU DIDN'T EXPECT.`

segments.voice: First, a scene from the book of Acts. Paul, the Christian apostle, stands in Athens before a crowd of Greek philosophers. He's there to speak about the God of Israel and about Jesus, and in the middle of it he quotes their own poets back to them. In the King James words: "For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring." He found a line worth repeating in someone else's tradition, and he named where it came from. Second, why naming matters. Paul didn't pretend the line was his. He said: your poets said this. That's a small act of honesty, and also a kind of thanks. It's the rule this path has kept all year: every teaching keeps its own name on it, and no voice is folded into another. Third, a man who thanked people by name. Marcus Aurelius opened his private notebook, known as the Meditations, with a list. From his grandfather he learned good character and an even temper. From his mother, generosity and simple living. From a teacher, to bear hardship and want little. On it goes, person after person, each with one thing learned. He never ranked them. He just named them. Fourth, what surprise does. A voice you expected can confirm what you already know. One you didn't expect can stretch you. It doesn't mean leaving where you stand, or changing who you are. It means someone from another room handed you something, and it fit.
screen: `PAUL QUOTES THE GREEK POETS.` · `YOUR POETS SAID THIS.` · `MARCUS THANKS EACH TEACHER BY NAME.` · `SURPRISE STRETCHES YOU.` · then, large: `THE SURPRISE.`

segments.voice: Let this year's voices pass by in your mind, and wait for the one that tugs a little, the line that surprised you. Name it, out loud or silently: the line, whose it was and where it came from, the way Paul named the poets and Marcus his teachers. 1057.title: Teachers of the year
1057.hook: Job, Patacara, Julian, Frankl, Rabia, Kabir, Thérèse, Corrie ten Boom
1057.howItsDone: People on many paths keep their teachers close by retelling their stories, reading their words, and remembering them by name; some write letters to teachers they never met as a way of saying what they learned.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Marcus Aurelius, and your line was the surprise. Today the voices get faces.

Who would you hire to teach a class on hard things? Not a man in the ashes, scraping himself with broken pottery. Or a young mother wandering a road with nothing left. Or a woman so ill the people at her bed think she's dying. Or a prisoner in a camp, holding on to one reason to get through the night. A strange faculty. Yet when this year's questions got hard, these were the people who did the teaching: eight of them.
screen: `THE ASHES. A ROAD. A SICKBED. A CAMP.` → `A STRANGE FACULTY.` → `EIGHT TEACHERS.`

segments.voice: First, the ones who grieved out loud. Job loses his children, his wealth and his health, and won't accept his friends' tidy explanations. At the end, God tells those friends: "ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath." The one who argued spoke rightly. Patacara, as the Buddhist commentary tells it, loses her family and wanders out of her mind with grief. She meets the Buddha, comes back to herself, becomes a nun, and in time a teacher of others. Second, the ones who held on inside the pain. Julian of Norwich, in her showings, wondered why sin had not been prevented, and heard: "all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well." Viktor Frankl, writing after the camps, argued that one freedom can't be taken from a person: the freedom to choose an attitude. Neither pretended the pain was small. Third, the ones who loved and forgave without bargaining. In a story people tell, Rabia of Basra walks with a torch and a bucket of water, to burn paradise and put out hell, so that God is loved for God alone. Kabir, in a verse kept in the Guru Granth Sahib, says that where there is forgiveness, there is God. Fourth, the ones who made it small and kept it hard. Thérèse of Lisieux called hers a little way: no great deeds, just the smallest things, done out of love. Corrie ten Boom, whose sister died in Ravensbrück, writes in The Hiding Place of a former guard holding out his hand, and of taking it. Eight teachers from many paths, each still exactly who they are, none asked to agree with the others.
screen: `JOB AND PATACARA: GRIEF, OUT LOUD.` · `JULIAN AND FRANKL: HOLDING ON INSIDE IT.` · `RABIA AND KABIR: NO BARGAINING.` · `THÉRÈSE AND CORRIE: SMALL, AND HARD.` · then, large: `MY TEACHERS.`
